title: Your landing page doesn't need more visits. It needs to understand why people don't convert.
description: Before asking for more traffic or redesigning the page, figure out where in the journey people give up and why.

related.title: Clint Acquire
related.body: In practice: a landing page and a conversational flow designed from the funnel and conversion metrics.

blocks.text: A landing page can get thousands of visits and still deliver very little.

In that scenario, the first reaction is usually to ask for more traffic, change the button color or redo the layout. But there's an earlier question: where in the experience are we losing people, and why?
Before redesigning a page, we need to understand the behavior the data is showing.
Conversion is the result of a journey

The conversion rate is usually calculated by dividing the number of conversions by the number of eligible visitors and multiplying the result by 100. But that number alone doesn't explain what happened.
Imagine a landing page that gets 10,000 sessions and generates 300 leads. Conversion is 3%. That figure describes the result, but it doesn't automatically point to the cause.

Maybe the ad promises a free demo, but the page talks about paid consulting. Maybe the headline doesn't explain the product's value. Maybe the form asks for too much information. Or maybe a good chunk of the traffic has no real intention to buy.
The rate shows there's a result. The diagnosis starts when we cross that result with other evidence.
Read the funnel before touching the interface
A first analysis can split the journey into stages:

steps.q: does the message grab attention and attract the right audience?
does the page load well and keep the ad's promise?
does the person quickly understand what's being offered?
do they find benefits, proof and answers to relevant doubts?
can they complete the form or click the CTA without trouble?
does the lead generated have potential to move forward in the sales process?

blocks.text: That split keeps us from treating every problem as a UI problem.

If the ad's CTR is low, maybe the message or targeting needs another look. If the ad gets clicks but the page loses visitors quickly, look into speed, consistency with the promise and relevance of the content. If many people start the form and few finish it, look into form friction.
Combine quantitative metrics with qualitative evidence
Some indicators help locate opportunities:

items: CTR: the share of people who click a link or ad after seeing it.
Landing page conversion rate: the share of visitors who complete the defined action.
Form starts and completions: show where people abandon.
Bounce or engagement rate: help understand visit quality, as long as you know how the tool defines it.
Cost per lead and cost per qualified lead: connect the page to spend and to sales quality.
Conversion by channel and device: help spot differences between traffic sources and between mobile and desktop experiences.

blocks.text: Then use session recordings, heatmaps, interviews, usability tests and feedback from the sales team to investigate possible causes. A heatmap can suggest where people click, but on its own it doesn't explain why they click or why they give up.
Don't optimize the wrong metric
A page can increase the number of leads and, at the same time, lower their quality. That's why conversion shouldn't be analyzed in isolation.

If the goal is to generate sales opportunities, also track the share of qualified leads, meetings booked, opportunities created and attributed revenue. The best result isn't necessarily capturing more contacts. It's generating more value from the traffic you have.

It's also worth separating user sessions from conversion events. The same person can visit several times or convert more than once. The denominator's definition needs to be consistent for the comparison to make sense.
A simple process to get started

items: Define the main conversion and confirm tracking works.
Break the journey into measurable stages.
Identify the biggest drop or the biggest business opportunity.
Write hypotheses that can be checked.
Change one thing at a time when possible.
Assess the effect on the main metric and on the guardrail metrics.
Record what you learned, even when the hypothesis isn't confirmed.

blocks.text: External benchmarks can serve as a reference, but they don't replace the page's own baseline. Reports like Unbounce's Conversion Benchmark Report show differences between industries and traffic types, reinforcing that any comparison has to consider context. The median Unbounce reports for its set of pages shouldn't be turned into a universal target for every business.
The useful question isn't just “what's my conversion rate?”. It's: which part of the journey is keeping the visitor's intent from turning into a valuable action?
